articles.body:
Celular com sistema Android — Foto: Andrey Matveev/Pexels

Comprar um celular Android intermediário em 2026 exige atenção a alguns pontos da ficha técnica que fazem diferença no uso diário.

Mais do que olhar só para os megapixels da câmera ou para o preço, o ideal é buscar um aparelho equilibrado, com bom desempenho, espaço interno suficiente e que possa ter uma vida útil mais longa.

A memória RAM influencia diretamente na fluidez do aparelho. Em 2026, 8 GB são o mínimo recomendado para usar redes sociais, aplicativos de mensagens, navegador e multitarefa sem travamentos frequentes.

Modelos com 12 GB ou mais de RAM também estão mais comuns e podem ser uma vantagem para quem joga no celular ou quer manter bom desempenho por mais tempo.

O espaço interno ganhou importância porque o Android, os aplicativos e os arquivos pessoais ocupam cada vez mais memória do celular.

Com 256 GB, o usuário tem mais espaço para guardar fotos, vídeos, documentos e até alguns jogos sem precisar apagar conteúdo com frequência.

Para quem pretende ficar anos com o aparelho, essa capacidade tende a ser mais adequada.

A bateria continua sendo um dos itens mais importantes para a maioria das pessoas.

Em celulares intermediários, 5.000 mAh já é o patamar considerado seguro para aguentar até um pouco mais de um dia inteiro de uso longe da tomada.

Vale checar ainda se a bateria usa tecnologia de silício-carbono, que permite aos fabricantes adotar maiores capacidades de carga em aparelhos mais finos. Já estão disponíveis nas lojas modelos com mais de 6.000 mAh, atingindo até 10.001 mAh.

A qualidade da tela interfere diretamente na experiência de uso. Painéis com tecnologia AMOLED ou equivalentes costumam oferecer cores mais vivas, melhor contraste e pretos mais profundos.

Já a taxa de atualização de 120 Hz deixa a navegação mais fluida, com rolagem mais suave e animações mais rápidas.

O tempo de suporte do Android e das atualizações de segurança virou um critério importante na compra de celulares.

Isso porque atualizações de segurança e novas versões do Android ajudam a manter o aparelho protegido e compatível com aplicativos mais recentes.

O recomendado é escolher modelos com pelo menos cinco anos de suporte. Em alguns intermediários, a Samsung já oferece seis anos de updates. Outras marcas, como a Motorola, variam de 2 a 7 anos, dependendo do modelo. Consulte o site do fabricante.

NFC é um termo interessante para checar antes da compra – é a tecnologia usada em pagamentos por aproximação, mas nem todos os celulares mais em conta oferecem o recurso.

Veja a seguir uma lista de celulares Android da categoria dos intermediários com as principais características listadas acima.

Os preços, consultados na última semana de outubro, iam de R$ 2.100 a R$ 7.000.

articles.title: Inside Facebook’s election war room
articles.summary: In a Menlo Park conference room, a global effort to fight misinformation comes together
articles.body: Information war, meet the war room. Facebook on Wednesday briefed reporters on its latest efforts to uncover nefarious uses of the platform during election season, offering a tour of the large conference room where dozens of employees are monitoring events around the clock. “We know when it comes to an elections, every moment counts,” said Samidh Chakrabarti, head of civic engagement at Facebook, who oversees the war room. “So if there are late-breaking issues we see on the platform, we need to be able to detect and respond to them in real time, as quickly as possible.” On one hand, the war room is just one of many conference rooms in MPK 20, the company’s Menlo Park, CA headquarters. But it’s larger than average, and has been stuffed with people and electronics equipment. There are desks for 24 people, and the room is ringed with 17 screens, each of which highlights a different stream of information Facebook is monitoring. [Image: Employees look for suspicious spikes in spam and hate speech, in some cases using custom software built for the purpose. They look for efforts at voter suppression, such as falsely telling people that lines are long or that the election has been delayed. (The team recently uncovered one such hoax claiming that the Brazilian election date had been delayed a day due to protests, and swiftly removed the offending posts.) Sign up for The Interface Get The Verge’s daily newsletter about social networks and democracy the night before everyone else does. Sign up Other employees use CrowdTangle, a company acquired by Facebook that monitors the viral spread of articles across platforms, to detect which articles are trending on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and Reddit. All told, representatives from 20 teams have people in the war room, representing 20,000 global employees working on safety and security. The teams include threat intelligence, data science, engineering, research, operations, legal, policy, communications, and representatives from Facebook-owned WhatsApp and Instagram. [Image: If anyone finds a problem, they escalate it to a specialist, who can then route it to the appropriate decision-maker. Facebook has also given state attorneys general and other elected officials a way to reach the war room quickly to report voter suppression and other suspicious activity. If the room is new, the work is not: Facebook teams have been working to fight misinformation in a coordinated way since 2016. The decision to bring them all together into a single room was made in the hopes that it would let them make decisions faster. “When every moment counts, then decision-making needs to be fast,” Chakrabarti sayd. “There’s no substitute for face to face, in-room interaction. so we felt [the need for] this physical war room to be able to coordinate teams.” On the day we visited, the room was decorated with a mix of American and Brazilian flags, in a nod to the next two elections that are being watched in the war room. It’s a fraught time: last week, Facebook removed 559 pages and 251 accounts in the United States for using fake identities and coordinating information campaigns. Meanwhile, Brazilian researchers today published the results of a study that examined the most-shared images in popular public WhatsApp chats and found that many of them contained misinformation: > From a sample of more than 100,000 political images that circulated in those 347 groups, we selected the 50 most widely shared. They were reviewed by Agência Lupa, which is Brazil’s leading fact-checking platform. Eight of those 50 photos and images were considered completely false; 16 were real pictures but used out of their original context or related to distorted data; four were unsubstantiated claims, not based on a trustworthy public source. This means that 56 percent of the most-shared images were misleading. Only 8 percent of the 50 most widely shared images were considered fully truthful. Facebook wouldn’t commit to keeping the war room open over forever. But with multiple elections taking place around the world each year, the company plans to keep it open for the foreseeable future. “This is going to be a constant arms race,” said Katie Harbath, Facebook’s global politics and government outreach director. “This is our new normal. Bad actors are going to get more sophisticated in what they’re doing, and we’re going to have to get more sophisticated in trying to catch them.”

articles.title: MacBook Pro rumor points to OLED, touchscreen upgrades next year
articles.summary: A Bloomberg report claims Apple’s next major MacBook Pro revision will add touch screens and OLED displays in late 2026 or early 2027.
articles.body: Apple just announced 14-inch MacBook Pro updates that add a new generation M5 processor, faster storage, and a promise of 24-hour battery life, but Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman now reports next year’s refresh will be more thorough. For several years, Gurman has said that, according to his sources, the next major MacBook Pro revamp would add touchscreens, OLED displays, and a lighter, thinner frame. He reported last month that nothing has changed about that plan other than pushing it back from a late 2025 launch due to OLED supply issues, and today, he expanded on those rumors with details of codenames (K114 and K116) and other specs. While Windows laptops have had touchscreens for years, Apple has avoided them, instead adding the Touch Bar to its machines for a few years before changing course in 2021. The report also teases another change that’s already a Windows feature but absent on Macs — a shift from Touch ID fingerprint scanning to Face ID authentication, which he says is still years away. Before that, he says we should still expect to see M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro updates with the current design released early next year. Similarly, updated versions of the MacBook Air, Mac Studio, Mac Mini, and two monitors are in the works. According to Gurman, the new MacBook Pros will contain M6 series Apple processors, a hole-punch style integrated webcam that’s more like the iPhone’s front-facing camera with its Dynamic Island, and reinforced hinges that don’t bounce around or shift while using the touchscreen. The bad news? Those changes are expected to increase the prices by “a few hundred dollars,” and they’re unlikely to reach Apple’s cheaper laptops the first time around.

articles.title: The Halide app’s anti-algorithm camera mode looks better with a little processing
articles.summary: Halide’s second-gen Process Zero upgrades might seem counterintuitive, but they’re enough to bring a skeptic around to the no-AI camera app.
articles.body: Something happens every time I try to use an iPhone camera like a real camera. Here’s how it goes: I shoot RAW in addition to the default HEIC output, and since I have the RAW file I might as well edit it to my taste. And if I’m going to do that, I want to use Lightroom on my MacBook. You know, real software. Then I remember: iPhone photos hate real software. Moving image files between devices is mysterious. If I Airdrop them to my MacBook will the HDR gain map tag along? Why do my photos always come out of Lightroom looking different than my edit? Where did that gain map go? I lack the patience to find out, so I just live with what my phone camera produces on its own and leave the heavy lifting to my “real” camera. This has its pros and cons. On the plus side, it’s way easier to deal with iPhone photos if they never leave the native camera app. But it also means leaving processing up to the iPhone, which tends to run amok with sharpening and raising shadows. I lean on the app’s built-in Photographic Styles (shout out to Rich Contrast, you’re a real one) to avoid this, but lots of people look to third party options like Halide’s Process Zero. Halide introduced this mode to its popular iPhone camera app last year. Process Zero promises to strip away the excess processing the native camera pipeline applies to images, resulting in photos with deeper shadows and less aggressive sharpening. Sounds great if you’re sick of the processed-to-death phone camera look! [Media: But I’ll admit to being a bit of a Process Zero skeptic. I lived through the pre-computational-photography era of crappy phone cameras, and I generally prefer the lower noise and usable low light photos you get with current camera tech. With a higher contrast photo style applied, it gets me close enough to the look I like, even if it feels like I’m taking pictures with a computer and not so much a camera. But Halide just released the second version of Process Zero in beta, adding a couple of features that got me interested: HDR support, and the ability to shoot in Apple’s RAW format. If those sound antithetical to Process Zero’s whole deal, well, maybe they are. And if we’re being technical about it, there was already some processing going on in Process Zero — there’s no other way to turn a bunch of sensor data into a usable image. But here’s what I appreciate about version two’s upgrades. First of all, adding HDR support doesn’t mean it’s going to turn your photo into a Thomas Kinkade painting. It means that the brightest areas of your photo can be brighter, creating a greater contrast between light and dark areas of the image. It’s the exact opposite of the flat, HDR-ish look that phone cameras often produce to try and represent a wide range of tones for an SDR screen. Don’t take my word for it; listen to Marc Levoy, who pioneered computational photography on smartphones. [Media: There’s also the option to shoot HEIC + RAW, meaning that in addition to the Process Zero image, you’ll have a DNG file that has been through some of Apple’s computational pipeline. Apple’s ProRAW format combines multiple frames to reduce noise, but retains all of the extra data you’d expect a RAW file to contain so you can apply your preferred tone mapping. You can turn this additional RAW capture on or off, and it doesn’t affect the Process Zero output, so you can treat it like a failsafe if you don’t like the default image. Whether or not you shoot RAW, you’ll have an option to adjust tone mapping within the Halide app through a new feature called Tone Fusion. It essentially boosts shadows, but it’s in your control and it’s not as intense as Apple’s tendencies. Even when I crank it all the way up, it doesn’t try to shift a blown-out sky blue the way the native iPhone processing does, and I appreciate that. [Image: [Image: [Image: I think an underrated benefit of Process Zero, or Adobe’s Project Indigo, is what it does for your mindset as you take photos. Sure, you could achieve the same kind of look by shooting with ProRAW in the native camera app, taking the photo into Lightroom, and adjusting contrast to your liking. But Process Zero provides appealing results straight out of the camera; it feels different knowing you’re going to get something you like right away, rather than a file you have to fight with first. I also feel like it gives me permission to think of myself as a photographer for a little while, not just a person with a phone. I went on a little photo walk in Seattle’s Pioneer Square and International District neighborhoods, which I’ve done dozens of times over the past decade. Outside Union Station — an old train station-turned-transit-agency-headquarters — I noticed a sign I’d never seen before, noting that the building’s great hall was open to the public. I’m not sure I would have bothered if I was just out wandering around, but with a specialized camera app on my phone I felt more like I was out doing photography, so I went in. It’s stunning, as it turns out, and I don’t know how I went over a decade living in this city without setting foot inside. And you know what? I do like the photos I got in there with Process Zero. Shooting with a ProRAW file in my back pocket, I knew I’d have something to work with if I didn’t like the default. But I haven’t touched those files, because the JPEGs are great. There was some late afternoon sun illuminating the station’s massive windows; rather than trying to bring those highlights down and boost every shadow, Process Zero lets the bright spots clip and keeps the emphasis on the interior. The HDR gain map lets the brightest parts of the scene pop, creating contrast between the fully illuminated windows and the slightly-less-bright golden sunlight filtering in against the wall. HDR is good, y’all. Process Zero v2 is part of a public preview of Halide’s larger Mark III update, so things might change before it’s finalized. But I like what I’m seeing, especially for Process Zero. The computational photography era has offered us a lot more than some over-processed JPEGs — the fact that we can take decent photos in basically any light conditions with the tiny sensors on our phones is nothing short of a technological triumph. Updating Process Zero to incorporate some of those benefits, if and when you want them, doesn’t detract from the minimalist experience; it’s an enhancement. And it’s enough to convert a skeptic like me.

articles.title: X product chief Nikita Bier is leaving after one year
articles.summary: Nikita Bier is stepping down as X’s head of product after just over a year in the role.
articles.body: X head of product Nikita Bier is stepping down and says he will move into a role as an advisor, writing that “it’s time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster.” He shared the update just over a month after celebrating his one-year anniversary on the job, and just weeks after Elon Musk’s combined SpaceX / X / xAI companies went public. He says that “almost every aspect of X” has been rebuilt while he was head of product, including its timeline, Android app, chat, and notifications. Going forward, the “next leaders” mentioned are Benji Taylor leading design with iOS lead Jonah Katz and Mridul Singhai leading the product team. [Media: Bier also called out the long-delayed and recently-launched X Money, which Elon Musk at one point expected to launch by the end of 2024. During his tenure, X has continued to focus on incentivizing native posts and login requirements for access to features, and last month Bier said that missing data from the X algorithm had made the platform feel like a “battleground.” Bier previously co-founded the startups tbh (acquired by Meta) and Gas (acquired by Discord). He was appointed to lead product just days before former X CEO Linda Yaccarino stepped down, and has been a public face of the company ever since.

articles.title: Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra update fixes reboot and display bugs
articles.summary: Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra was blighted by some nuisance bugs at launch, but now the company has released a firmware update to resolve them.
articles.body: Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra was blighted by some nuisance bugs at launch, but now the company has released some new firmware to resolve them. The October 22nd release addresses three notable issues in particular: screen flickering, unexpected restarts, and lengthy reboot times alongside unspecified “additional bug fixes and general performance improvements,” according to Microsoft’s announcement. My colleague Tom Warren experienced some of these issues when he reviewed the Surface Laptop Ultra, finding that rebooting the device was “surprisingly slow” and that “moving a window around rapidly sometimes left a little trail.” He also ran into some speaker interference issues that were “loud enough to sound like firecrackers” and resolved them upon rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra, but found that “it’s happened a couple of times now.” We’ve asked Microsoft if this is one of the additional bug fixes included in the update. In its announcement, Microsoft says some additional steps “may be required” for Surface Laptop Ultra users after installing this firmware update: > We recommend that you restart your Surface to complete any remaining part of the installation. To restart your device, select Start, and then select Power > Restart. The firmware update will be delivered to all Surface Laptop Ultra devices, but not every device will receive it at the same time. If you don’t want to wait around, you can manually install the update by following the instructions over on Microsoft’s driver and firmware page. The firmware update can’t be uninstalled or reverted to an earlier version.

articles.title: T-Mobile’s new plans include swappable subscription perks
articles.summary: T-Mobile’s new “T-Mix” plans start at $55 / month and come with the ability to switch between subscriptions to services like Netflix and Apple TV.
articles.body: T-Mobile is launching new “T-Mix” plans that bundle wireless service with subscriptions to services like Netflix, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, device promotions, and more, as reported earlier by Fierce Network. The Standard plan starts at $55 / month (with autopay) for one line and one “Pick,” which you can change up to four times during the year without changing the cost of your plan. The Standard also offers up to 50GB of “premium” data, video streaming in 480p, unlimited 3G hotspot connectivity, and unlimited 2G in Canada and Mexico. Meanwhile, the mid-tier More plan starts at $75 / month for one line, two Picks per line, and unlimited data. It also adds up to 4K UHD video streaming, up to 60GB of high-speed hotspot data, and up to 15GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico. [Image: The highest-tier Loaded plan, which starts at $95 / month for one line, bumps things up a little more, offering access to up to three Picks per line for the first three lines (T-Mobile caps this plan at 11 perks in total). The Loaded plan also comes with the same up to 4K UHD video streaming benefit, as well as up to 250GB of high-speed hotspot data and up to 30GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico. The types of perks you can add vary depending on how many your plan supports: * One Pick: Apple TV, DashPass by DoorDash, Google AI Plus, Hulu with ads, Netflix Standard with ads, Pandora Plus, Paramount Plus Essential, SiriusXM All Access (app only), YouTube Premium Lite, 500 miles / month through Delta SkyMiles, T-Satellite * Two Picks: Apple Music Individual, Google AI Pro, Pandora Premium, Xbox Game Pass Premium, YouTube Premium * Three Picks: Netflix Standard, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate * Four Picks: ESPN Unlimited, Netflix Premium As noted by CNET, you can also trade your Picks for discounts on a new phone. T-Mobile says that you can change up your perks every 90 days, according to Fierce Network. However, T-Mobile notes that how often you can change your perks depends on the benefit that you choose. “Some benefits let you switch any time, others hold your Picks for a quarter or longer,” T-Mobile says, adding that some services will charge if you switch them outside the change window. T-Mobile also offers an annual selection period where you can reset all of your perks.

articles.title: Walter Koenig, the Russian Crewman Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
articles.summary: He joined the TV series for the second season but had more to do on another acclaimed sci-fi program, 'Babylon 5.'
articles.body:
Walter Koenig, the boyish actor who remains an integral part of Star Trek lore thanks to his portrayal of the Russian crewman Pavel Chekov, has died. He was 90.

Koenig, also known for playing the scoundrel Alfred Bester on another sci-fi space series, Warner Bros. Television's Babylon 5 , died Sunday of natural causes in his home in North Hollywood, his rep announced.

Raised in Manhattan as a son of Lithuanian immigrants, Koenig joined Gene Roddenberry's Star Trek for the start of its second season and appeared on 36 of the 50 episodes that aired in 1967-68 and 1968-69. He also portrayed Pavel Andreievich Chekov in the first seven Paramount movies, released from 1979 through 1991, that emanated from the NBC show.

In a 2013 interview for the TV Academy Foundation, Koenig said he didn't watch Star Trek before he came aboard. "I'd flip through the channels and I'd see Styrofoam rocks — they were so obviously Styrofoam — and I said, 'This has got to be phony.' I didn't give it a chance," he recalled.

The actor portrayed a Russian for the first time in his career — a student who had defected to the U.S. — on a 1963 episode of the NBC drama Mr. Novak .

He then guest-starred as a young sergeant whose goal of being promoted to officer is complicated by the fact that his mother is a communist on a 1964 installment of The Lieutenant , another series created by Roddenberry.

After his Star Trek audition, Koenig spent a couple of lonely hours in an outer office wondering if he had gotten the job when he was approached by a man and asked to follow him into the wardrobe room.

"He drops on his knees in front of me," Koenig said, "and takes my crotch in his hand, and I'm saying, 'What are you doing?!" I didn't see the tape-measuring ruler in his other hand, and he was measuring from my crotch to my cuff to decide how long my pants should be. He says, 'You do have to have a costume, don't you?'

"And that's the auspicious way I learned I was on Star Trek and it was going to change my life."

Marvin Walter Koenig was born in Chicago on Sept. 14, 1936. His father, a translator for RCA Victor and later an entrepreneur, was a "dyed-in-the wool commie," Koenig said. He noted that FBI agents once searched his family's apartment.

Koenig starred in productions of Peer Gynt and The Devil's Disciple at Fieldston High School in New York, went to Grinnell (Iowa) College to study pre-med and then transferred to UCLA after his sophomore year, pursuing a degree in psychology.

However, he took an acting class and received a letter of recommendation from his teacher that in 1958 got him into the famed Neighborhood Playhouse in New York, where he studied alongside James Caan , Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman .

The boyish actor returned to L.A. to claim a role in the 1961 Burt Lancaster film The Young Savages (1961), but that job fell through. He then made his onscreen debut on the afternoon show Day in Court and appeared in the pilot and the first two episodes of General Hospital in 1963.

At the time, Koenig excelled at doing various dialects, portraying French, Armenian, Swedish and German characters, as well as playing juvenile delinquents, as he did in 1964 on The Alfred Hitchcock Hour . The episode was directed by Joseph Pevney and written by Harlan Ellison — later, two prominent behind-the-scenes players on Star Trek .

In fact, Pevney was one of the people for whom Koenig auditioned for Chekov.

"He really liked my work, he kept telling me, 'You're going to be a big star,'" Koenig recalled. "When I came in to read for Star Trek , he was very enthusiastic and one of the reasons I got the part."

Koenig said the character he was to play was at first named Jones because producers wanted an actor that would appeal to the same demographic that Davy Jones of The Monkees did — kids 8- to 14-years-old.

"And indeed, my [fan] mail was from people who were 8- to 14-years-old," he said. "They said, "I think you're groovy, I love your hair' — which was a wig, by the way. I got hundreds and hundreds of letters, the third most after Bill [Shatner] and Leonard [Nimoy ]."

He said Chekov would eventually become less popular because of three things — "the hair wasn't real; I wasn't really Russian, and that exotic flavor was gone; and [viewers found out] that I was married, and they couldn't fantasize about being with Chekov. Things then started to take a nosedive."

On the series, Chekov really didn't have much to do; the actor knew he was there to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill in it."

Koenig was more important to the Star Trek movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).

In 1976, Koenig and Shatner both appeared on an episode of Columbo , but the Star Trek veterans didn't share any scenes and didn't talk during production. "It was between the series and the movies, and I don't think he remembered my name," Koenig said.

He also said he "really upset" when he was left out of Star Trek: The Animated Series because of budgetary reasons. Koenig did write an episode for the 1973-74 NBC cartoon.

He played Chekov again as "The Admiral," age 143, in the two-part, crowdsourced Renegades series that debuted online in 2017.

Worried about not getting work after Star Trek was canceled, he began writing and penned episodes for The Powers of Matthew Star , Family , Land of the Lost and The Incredible Hulk . He also wrote, produced and starred in the sci-fi film InAlienable (2010), starring Richard Hatch.

Koenig lost out on a chance to appear in Babylon 5 when he suffered a heart attack and had a quadruple bypass in 1993, but series creator J. Michael Straczynski wrote the part of Bester for him when he was healthy enough to act again. Unlike Chekov, that character was multidimensional and key to several storylines.

He wrote the memoir Warped Factors‚ A Neurotic's Guide to the Universe , published in 1998, then expanded on that for Beaming Up and Getting Off , released in 2020.

Koenig married actress Judy Levitt, who appeared with him in three Star Trek movies and on Babylon 5 , in July 1965, and they were together until her death in December 2022 at age 83. Their son, Andrew, who played Richard "Boner" Stabone on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains , died by suicide in 2010 at age 41.

Survivors include his daughter, actress and screenwriter Danielle Koenig ( Star vs. the Forces of Evil ).

articles.title: Nothing’s eye-catching Ear 3A earbuds are matching their best price to date
articles.summary: Nothing’s feature-rich Ear 3A are on sale for $79 ($20 off) at multiple retailers right now, matching the lowest price we’ve seen on the noise-canceling earbuds.
articles.body: If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a lot of features for the price, and they’re an even better value now that all four colors are on sale at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy for $79 ($20 off), matching their all-time low price. [Product: Nothing Ear 3A earbuds | The Ear 3A deliver great performance for the price, with extensive EQ options that let you fine-tune the sound to your liking. My colleague John Higgins found the default sound a little too bass-heavy, but appreciated how easy it was to adjust — which is great, since that level of customization is unusual for earbuds at this price. While they won’t completely drown out chatter of your local coffee shop, the ANC does a good job of quieting low drones, including air conditioners and airplane cabin noise. We did encounter some bugs in testing, however, including abrupt changes in noise cancellation levels when using adaptive ANC, as well as occasional issues with voice calls in noisy environments. Still, they’re relatively minor drawbacks given what you get for the price. The Ear 3A also come in some fun colors — including a striking pink shade — and each pair includes extra-small ear tips for a more comfortable fit. They even offer a shortcut to access ChatGPT and include 32MB of built-in storage, letting you record up to two hours of a phone call and transfer the recording through the companion app. Read our Nothing Ear 3A review.

articles.title: Halide’s Duo update just knocked an item off my camera wish list.
articles.summary:

articles.title: Uh oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren't happy about it | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A small number of early adopters of the much hyped new foldable phone from Apple have complained of screens cracking.
articles.body:
The launch of the iPhone Duo , Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.

Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining that about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by appearance a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.

404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company old Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”

Creating a functional foldable phone has been long been an ambition in Silicon Valley but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies . Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

articles.title: iPhone Duo screens are cracking, and they have one thing in common
articles.summary: Less than a week after launch, iPhone Duo owners are reporting cracked inner screens.
articles.body:
Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, officially began shipping to customers last week, and we're starting to see why folding screens are difficult to get right. A significant number of reports have surfaced online from early iPhone Duo buyers who have had the inner screen crack. The interesting part? They're all breaking in the exact same spot.

Impacted devices show a bright band of white pixels extending from the same point near the middle of the fold in the display. A Reddit user said they felt something in the hinge as they were opening it, right before the issue appeared on their screen — and after only six hours of owning it. To Apple's credit, the user says the company replaced it immediately with a new Duo when he took it to a nearby Apple Store.

the iPhone Duo might have CrackGate issue there are so many cases of it on Reddit where it's breaking in the exact same place pic.twitter.com/IlCJj8kJ8B — Holly - I like tech (@AnxiousHolly) October 24, 2026

the iPhone Duo might have CrackGate issue there are so many cases of it on Reddit where it's breaking in the exact same place pic.twitter.com/IlCJj8kJ8B

Holly - I like tech (@AnxiousHolly) October 24, 2026

The folks at iFixit, which is known for tearing down new devices to show how they work, may have found the issue causing the defective screens. "The damage we're seeing in photos isn't right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends," iFixit says in its iPhone Duo teardown . It goes on to speculate that the center support bar under the fold doesn't drop down far enough and may create "a small stress hotspot near the reported break location."

In a statement to 9to5Mac , Apple said the issue impacts "a small number" of devices. "The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

It's unclear how many devices the defect may impact. However, this sort of issue isn't exactly new to foldable screens; the original Samsung Galaxy Fold showed a similar problem in The Verge's 2019 review .

"Apple said that any customer with problems should ask for a replacement, which is the right first step," Francisco Jeronimo, vice president of devices at analyst firm IDC , told Yahoo. "At $1,999, Apple is positioning the Duo as a premium alternative to established foldables, and how it handles this first-generation issue will shape buyer confidence in the category well beyond its own sales. Apple has a loyal customer base and a retail network that can swap devices on the spot, but with a further 28 markets launching on 30 October, it needs to clarify its warranty position quickly."

Foldable screens are complicated, involving complex hinge mechanisms and multiple delicate layers that must slide and flex past one another. Apple says its hinge mechanism has more than 100 components, while the screen is made up of 10 ultra-thin layers . A small defect with any one of those parts could cause problems. Other companies that make foldable phones have had years to work out the kinks with their manufacturing process, but it's clear Apple still has some work to do with its first foldable.

articles.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Star Calls Adam Brody’s Pro-Palestine Comments ‘Right Out of Hitler’s Playbook’
articles.summary: Another member of the "Nobody Wants This" team has chimed in on Adam Brody's remarks about Israel and Palestine.
articles.body:
Another member of the " Nobody Wants This " team has chimed in on Adam Brody's remarks about Israel and Palestine.

Tovah Feldshuh, who plays Bina Roklov (the mother of Brody's Rabbi Noah Roklov) on Erin Foster's Netflix series, spoke to The New York Post on Sunday about Brody's recent interview with GQ , in which he told a reporter about the Gaza war: "Put me down as thinking it's a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine."

"To accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild," Feldshuh said in response. "It's right out of Hitler's playbook. You take the victim and you make the victim the perpetrator."

Feldshuh did not mince words in her comments about her on-screen son, stating that it "makes a difference to the (Jewish) community" when accusations of genocide are made by Jewish actors like Brody. She also cited the political theory of the horseshoe effect, saying that "socialism and antisemitism are trying to meet" in the current political climate.

A representative for Brody did not immediately respond to TheWrap's request for comment.

"I believe that the perseverance of the existence of the state of Israel is crucial to the well-being of the democratic world and of the free world," Feldshuh said. "Of course, Israel needs the United States, (but) the United States needs Israel, believe you me."

Foster, who created "Nobody Wants This" and serves as showrunner alongside Craig DiGregorio, Jenni Konner and Bruce Eric Kaplan, recently chimed in on Brody's comments herself. In an exclusive clip shared by EW of the Oct. 27 episode of the podcast "Not Skinny But Not Fat," Foster called her feelings on the matter "complicated."

"I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing," she said. "And while I love Adam, I also disagree with him — and that's OK."

articles.summary: Apple has released iOS 27.2 for compatible iPhones, bringing fixes for more than 160 security vulnerabilities along with new features for Siri, Messages,
articles.body: Apple has released iOS 27.2 for compatible iPhones, bringing fixes for more than 160 security vulnerabilities along with new features for Siri, Messages, Photos and other apps. The update addresses issues that could allow malicious apps to access private information, bypass privacy settings or use hardware features such as the camera and Bluetooth without proper permission. Apple said none of the vulnerabilities covered by the update were actively exploited by attackers. The release also adds new options for Apple Music, Podcasts, FaceTime and the Apple TV app. Here is a look at the key changes and how to download the update.iOS 27.2 fixes over 160 security vulnerabilitiesA major part of the iOS 27.2 update focuses on protecting user data and improving app permissions. Apple has fixed vulnerabilities affecting several parts of the operating system, including Accounts, App Intents, Photos, Contacts, Calendar, Maps, Shortcuts and Siri.One fix addresses an issue that could allow apps to access private user information. Apple has also fixed a vulnerability in Hide My Email that could expose a user's original email address despite the feature being enabled. The update includes additional checks to stop apps from accessing users' Photos libraries or bypassing privacy preferences. It also addresses an issue that could allow certain apps to see which applications were installed on an iPhone.Other fixes prevent malicious apps from accessing the camera without permission or using Bluetooth without the required approval. Apple has also addressed security issues that could lead to denial-of-service attacks, unexpected app crashes and unauthorised code execution.According to the information provided by Apple, none of these vulnerabilities were actively exploited at the time of the update's release.iOS 27.2 brings new Siri and Messages featuresThe update adds improvements to Siri AI, allowing it to recall previous conversations and draw information from sources such as Messages attachments, Calendar event attendees and voicemails. Apple has also improved its use of Safari history and Reading List information.Users can now select and copy specific portions of a Siri response. A redesigned setting also makes it easier to choose which apps Siri, Search and suggestions can access.Siri AI support has expanded to include French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish. However, the feature is not available in the European Union or mainland China. Siri AI also requires an iPhone 15 Pro or a later model.In Messages, users can receive contextual suggestions, such as tracking a package or adding a dinner invitation to Calendar. They can choose which suggestions to enable, including Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Maps, and Flights and Packages.Other features in the iOS 27.2 updateThe update brings several other changes across Apple's apps and services:- Apple Music: The app gets a redesigned black-and-white icon, replacing the red design.- Photos: Users can edit captions and comments in Shared Albums, avoid duplicate photos and receive reminders before albums expire.- Podcasts: The Home tab now separates New Episodes from Continue Playing.- Apple TV: Users can create profiles on their iPhone and iPad, including child profiles with content-rating controls.- FaceTime: Group calls now support Dual Capture on compatible iPhones, allowing video from the front and rear cameras to be captured together. Users can also add a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call.- Apple TV app: Multiview lets users watch up to four live sports streams simultaneously for supported events.- Shortcuts: The update adds new actions and automation options, including an automation for when the iPhone Duo is opened or closed.The update also includes SynthID labelling for images created with Image Playground and certain edits made in Photos.How to download and install iOS 27.2Apple iPhone users can check for the update through their device's Settings app. Before installing, it is advisable to connect the phone to Wi-Fi and back up important data.Follow these steps to update your iPhone:Open Settings on your iPhone.Tap General.Select Software Update.If iOS 27.2 is available, tap Download and Install.Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the installation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo screen cracks; company says: “If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they...”
articles.summary: Apple has acknowledged that some iPhone Duo units are dealing with a cracked inner display, days after early buyers began sharing photos of screens
articles.body: Apple has acknowledged that some iPhone Duo units are dealing with a cracked inner display, days after early buyers began sharing photos of screens breaking along the hinge. The company says the problem affects “a small number of iPhone Duo units” and has asked users facing it to contact AppleCare for a replacement.Complaints began piling up on Reddit and social media soon after Apple’s first foldable went on sale on October 23. The damage looks almost identical across reports, with a vertical crack down the crease and a bright white band of dead pixels on the right side of the screen. For a device that costs Rs 2,99,900 in India, that is a rough start.Apple says the iPhone Duo display issue affects only a small number of unitsIn its statement provided to The Verge, Apple called the early response to the iPhone Duo “incredibly positive” and pointed to developers quickly updating their apps for its folding design. It did not say what is causing the cracks or how many units are affected.The most detailed account comes from an owner in Melbourne, Australia, who had the phone for about six hours and had opened it fewer than 20 times. While showing it to a friend, they felt something odd around the hinge underneath the screen, then heard an audible crack. The Apple Store replaced the unit on the spot, and the technician reportedly called it a day one manufacturing error.A Dallas owner says the hinge felt tight after about four folds, and pushing past it ended in a loud pop before setup was done. Images from Chinese social media, where the foldable reached buyers first, show damage in nearly the same spot, though some involve demo units with unknown histories.Sand, dirt and backward bends expose the iPhone Duo hinge’s weak spotsA durability test by YouTuber JerryRigEverything offers some clues. Piling sand and dirt into the phone eventually jammed the hinge, so it no longer closed fully. Bending it backwards left line faults on the inner display, though the hinge stopped it from snapping in half. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 kept its inner screen working after a similar test.Apple has also published a support page for hinge trouble, covering unexpected noises, a loose hinge and a device that won’t close fully. Hinge failures from normal use should fall under the one-year warranty, and buyers get 14 days to return the phone.Getting a replacement could be the harder part. Pre-orders sold out within minutes, and delivery dates now stretch to late January 2027. If that “small number” grows, swaps may not be as quick as the one in Melbourne.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sterling Anderson doesn’t think humanoid robots should be building cars
articles.summary: As EV demand shifts and competition from Tesla and Chinese automakers intensifies, GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson explains how the Detroit giant is betting on AI, centralized software, and autonomous tech to stay ahead.
articles.body: At a splashy event in New York City last week, General Motors unveiled its new tech roadmap centered on AI-driven vehicle development, advanced battery tech, high-powered car computers, and autonomous driving. Some of this was old news: We already knew the automaker was developing hands-free, eyes-off driving automation and had been prototyping new battery chemistries. In a sense, the real purpose of the event was to showcase how all these pieces fit together. With its new “intelligence-defined vehicle” paradigm, GM is banking on artificial intelligence, centralized computing, and virtualized engineering to cut vehicle development timelines in half, aiming to compress a typical four- to five-year process down to just over two. Yet, this high-tech overhaul arrives against a backdrop of steep industry headwinds and razor-thin margins for error. GM’s aggressive pivot comes as the automaker faces a wave of hyperefficient Chinese EV makers that are aggressively expanding globally. At the same time, softening EV demand in the US has forced GM to recalibrate its electrification hopes, balancing multibillion-dollar investments in next-generation battery plants with the ongoing costs of software development. To be sure, for GM to bet its future on unproven software architectures and autonomous technology is a high-stakes gamble: If these complex AI systems falter or if development hits delays, GM risks burning through massive amounts of money while falling further behind agile rivals (like Tesla) that were built as software-first companies from day one. After the event, I sat down with Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, to talk about the company’s risky new ventures as well as how he plans to steer a century-old Detroit giant through an increasingly fast, software-driven world. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. So this was quite the massive announcement — just lots of disparate pieces. Is there a unifying theme here, would you say? And if so, what do you think it is? The car’s getting smarter. That’s it? That’s it. I think so. Your vehicle is becoming a trusted, intelligent companion, and we’re doing that in a variety of ways. I think I might be one of the only guys who gets as excited as I do about what we’re doing in the development process and making that faster and better. I don’t know how many people are going to come away with that takeaway in quite the spirit that I think it merits, but the level of tests and performance optimality that we can achieve when we can spin design decisions hundreds of times — that previously would have accommodated one — is huge. It’s really huge. I’ve been asked now by two folks I’ve met afterwards, “Hey, what about safety, and does speed come at the cost of safety?” The way we are getting speed is by virtualizing tests in a way that allows us to improve safety. Historically, I would have been able to afford X prototypes that I could send to crash tests, and it took me six months. Now, I kick off thousands of tests in the virtual world that give me feedback much quicker. So I get speed, and I get safety, better coverage, and better understanding. There’s a lot of cake being eaten, too, in this process. "“I kick off thousands of tests in the virtual world that give me feedback much quicker.”" - Sterling Anderson What kind of AI models are you using? I know you talked about how data is sort of the currency here, so obviously there’s a lot that you’re pulling from your own customers, but there’s a range of products out there. What’s the dividing line between what to look for outside the company versus what to pull from inside? It’s a good question. It depends on what we’re doing with it. In many cases, the transformer-based foundation models enable some of the generative design stuff I was talking about — we have enough data in-house based on decades of design files, analyses, etc., that we can get a pretty well-trained system to express our data well. But we have access to — and anybody has access in many cases to — a lot of data that informs us. The co-training of these models with data that exists beyond GM’s walls tends to make them better. So we do it with all of them. You’ve talked about moving from deterministic code to probabilistic AI that learns from the structure of the world and from the data. How are you specifically embedding these models into the vehicles? How much is run locally versus pulling from the cloud? For any safety-critical functionality, the inference is done onboard because we can’t deal with latency, possible dropouts, or whatever else. Some of these examples you saw from the team earlier today, like the OnStar AI interactions, aren’t safety-critical. You probably noticed, given the latency, that you had some round-tripping happening there because we don’t need to run those all onboard. Now, we’re thinking about distilling them down into onboard models just to deal with the latency, but that’s an on-the-edge user experience element, not a core safety consideration. You talked a little bit during your presentation about how big GM is, which gives you advantages with data, but also a lot of inertia. Back in 2019, GM President Mark Reuss talked about moving toward the “digital brain” of the vehicle, and in 2021 you talked about Ultifi. Have things sped up now? Are you on the glide path at this point? Yeah, and a big enabler of it is that common electrical system, including centralized compute. Historically, I know of very few killers to software speed quite like complexity. The moment a software team has a very large set of deployment targets that don’t share a common baseline is the moment you slow that team down enormously. Rolling this out across our entire portfolio is specifically to enable software speed so we don’t have to continue to support vehicles of various configurations. As that hardware set rolls out, software engineers will suddenly be able to operate like they would if they were in a company with two models in production, which they just haven’t been able to in history. GM is unique in having this huge portfolio of brands with distinct identities. How do you decide what to standardize across every vehicle versus ensuring a Buick remains a Buick and a GMC Sierra remains unique? It’s a combination of things. First, the essence of each brand tends to manifest in aesthetics and interaction models. Aesthetics is something you can effectively skin via design, both in digital interfaces and physical sheet metal. We already do a fairly good job of commonizing the under-the-skin componentry because why wouldn’t we? For a given segment of vehicle, there’s a particular ride quality that tends to be best received by everybody. Our T1-2 platform for our next-generation trucks is common between brands. Where you’ll see us differentiate is in the feature set, the aesthetics, and interaction patterns we effectively skin segment by segment. Sales has dedicated brand channels, but engineering is all one organization. That ensures we don’t ship heterogeneous, suboptimal cars for different brands just because a team that was slightly worse was assigned to one brand or another. I want our engineering team focusing all of their effort on what is the absolute best suspension, powertrain, or drive unit, and then we scale it across the portfolio. Speaking of autonomy, we have autonomous vehicles on the road today — Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla Cybercabs. What are the challenges GM still needs to solve to get to a point where someone can take their eyes off the road comfortably and safely? When you say “eyes off,” you mean autonomous? Autonomously, yes. Hands off, mind off, eyes off. But at the same time, you wouldn’t be recommending people go to sleep in their vehicles yet? We are designing them such that should they fall asleep, it won’t be unsafe, because we don’t have the luxury of ensuring that they’re paying attention. The reason you won’t hear me use terms like “eyes off” is because I hear people use those terms in reference to nonsensical levels of automation. What do you think your mind is doing when your eyes are on your phone? Where’s your mind? Let’s not draw these nonsensical distinctions. If you believe that your driver assistance system is super capable, you are already at risk of complacency — at risk of treating it like it’s an autonomous system. Our philosophy is: If we’re going to design an autonomous system, we’re going to actually design an autonomous system. The path of incrementalism that we’ll take will work for personal ownership, not the one that worked for robotaxis. Instead of regionally specific, speed-limited settings, we’re going to go toward road-type specific settings and expand outward from there. They both converge in the same place — self-driving everywhere at all times — but take different paths to get there. With robotaxis today, we see problems around nuisance situations — like blocking intersections or emergency vehicles. Do you feel personal autonomy, as GM defines it, solves some of that because the driver remains an option to fall back on? The form of the fallback matters. We will not fall back in a safety-critical dynamic situation. It’s just not reasonable to do that. What we can do in a non-safety-critical situation — where the vehicle is stopped and something odd is happening — is hand it back to the driver once we’ve reached a safe place. Having a human in the loop is very useful for that. How do you structure that handoff to avoid driver complacency? We’re not handing back dynamically. This is not an exchange of “you drive, now I’ll drive, oops, I don’t recognize this.” This is not Level 3. In the same way you put a robotaxi in a bounded region, we will put personally owned autonomous vehicles on a particular road. When on that road, we will take the human to their destination and give a graceful countdown — like, “Hey, you’ve got 10 minutes left in this ride.” If they take over preemptively, great. Should they not take over, the system brings the vehicle to a safe state off the off-ramp and says, “I told you 10 minutes ago to take over. We’re stopped, and I’m not going any further.” You have to operate under the assumption that bad actors will try to abuse the system — sitting in the back seat, like we’ve seen with Tesla users. I get far more nervous when misuse happens in the context of a driver-assist system that wasn’t designed to handle every situation. If the vehicle accepts control, our system is designed to deal with more situations that can be thrown at it in that circumstance. So my anxiety level declines dramatically. Features like OnStar AI ask for access to calendars, emails, and personal data. Given past FTC orders regarding GM selling customer data to third-party brokers without permission, how do you ensure customers can trust you with this data? Privacy has to be designed in. With end-to-end encryption, we don’t see your data; you grant permission to an assistant that performs better with context. Data is only available to us at an aggregate, anonymized level. At an individual level, it is encrypted and under your control. When you buy a car, going through dozens of terms and conditions leads to “click, click, click” without reading, which does a disservice to trust. We have dramatically simplified these authorizations down to a couple of clear choices that explain why the car needs data — like reading your calendar for smart routing. You can revoke permission, delete your data, or port it out at any time. You alluded to trust, which is foundational. Decisions made in the past by people who no longer work for this company have an overhang, but that’s not the company we are today. We earn that trust back by designing the architecture so that even if someone made a bad decision internally, the system technically wouldn’t allow them to access raw user data. And the way we do that is by designing it. Look, even if we had someone stupid work for us again and do something like this, they couldn’t. They wouldn’t be able to access it. AI is cutting vehicle development times, but we’re also seeing hype around factory automation and humanoid robots from companies like Tesla and Rivian. Is GM heading in that direction? If you want to be perceived as a robotics player these days, it seems you have to have a humanoid robot that does backflips. It’s weird. Advocacy for humanoids often comes from people who historically advocate for first-principles engineering, but humanoids are not born from first principles. They put form over function. The logic assumes the human form factor is optimal for a factory floor, but this form factor evolved to run away from lions on the African savanna! Production environments weren’t built for human forms any more than roads built for horses meant cars should have four legs. The most valuable real estate in a factory is the floor. Having bumbling humanoid robots clamoring in and out of vehicles is not where you start. You start with form factors that look alien — like an octopus hanging from a gantry that reaches into a moving vehicle line. We’re ignoring the “religion” of humanoids and focusing on underlying AI intelligence that can operate various specialized robot form factors for specific tasks. Is GM building these robotics systems itself? We already are. We actively work with heavy machinery suppliers like Fanuc, but we are actively developing many of our own solutions. People are excited about cars getting smarter, but they also want them to be cheaper. How do these announcements lead to more affordable options? LMR (lithium manganese rich) battery chemistry is a huge part of this. It delivers a range close to high-nickel packs at a cost closer to LFP. On a per-range basis, a customer will be able to buy a fourth-gen GM EV for less money than a competitor’s profitable model without relying on subsidies. Additionally, commonizing our electrical architecture reduces wiring length and vehicle mass dramatically, making cars inherently more affordable. Virtualizing development cuts prototype costs, allowing vehicle business cases to clear at lower retail prices. This applies to ICE vehicles and hybrids as well, not just EVs. Will this intelligence lead to higher subscriptions and paywalls? Capability advances inevitably over time without raising financial costs — the device in your lap does far more than computers years ago for less money. Regarding subscriptions: I’m here to build great products. If customers like paying for services like a lease, let them; if not, don’t force them. [GM spokesperson Chaiti Sen: For immediate features like OnStar AI, it will be included in our basic package. We aren’t going to paywall core baseline experiences or hand customers a bare “tin shell.”] For your sensor suite, you’re using cameras, radar, and lidar. Do you see that remaining in perpetuity, or could you eventually scale back to a vision-only approach like Tesla? If you scale back to vision-only, physics suggests you’ll be in trouble in certain situations. Radar is so cheap that dropping it doesn’t make sense — dropping it is a weird religious stance that ignores physics. Lidar operates on a similar wavelength to visible light and helps co-train camera systems to get better faster. Cameras can’t see through dense fog or measure instantaneous velocity like radar can. Having a multisensor suite provides obvious safety advantages that physics simply demands.

articles.title: Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo 2 adds a touchscreen and video recording
articles.summary: Fujifilm is trying to find the right balance of fun and photography with its latest hybrid instant camera.
articles.body: Fujifilm is trying to find the right balance of fun and photography with its latest hybrid instant camera. Like its predecessor, the Instax Mini Evo 2 feels less like a retro gimmick, and more like a basic digital camera that just happens to have a built-in printer. It also enjoys some key upgrades: a larger 1/2.77-inch sensor compared to the 1/5-inch sensor on the first Mini Evo, a bigger 4.5-inch rear display with touchscreen controls, and basic video recording too — though only the few seconds leading up to a photo. Video is limited in other ways compared to modern standards — the MP4 clips can only be saved to a microSD card (though there is internal storage for photos), no audio is recorded, and quality is limited to 560 × 992 pixels and 24FPS, according to DPReview — but it’s still a feature we wouldn’t expect to see on an instant camera. This is also Fujifilm’s first Instax model to feature an LCD touchscreen, ditching the rear controls in favor of a larger display that takes up the entire back of the camera. Other physical controls have been preserved though, including two dials and a film-inspired print lever. You can use either the dials or touchscreen to access the 10 film and 10 lens effect options that were available on the first Instax Mini Evo, though the selection has changed slightly with this new model. There’s also an Expanded View mode that “gives users a wider field of view than the shooting area.” The camera charges via USB-C, prints 2 x 3-inch Instax Mini format photos, and lets you adjust the exposure, white balance, and flash settings on your snaps. [Media: The Instax Mini Evo 2 will be available for $290 and goes on sale at the end of November. Black is the only available color option, but it still retains the classic retro look that’ll probably land well with the youth market.

articles.title: AirFly’s wireless headphone dongle adds a screen to guide you through the pairing process
articles.summary: The new $80 Airfly View can connect two pairs of wireless headphones to an in-flight entertainment system using simplified instructions on its built-in screen.
articles.body: Twelve South has announced a new version of its Airfly dongle that simplifies the pairing process when connecting wireless headphones to devices that don’t natively support Bluetooth. Instead of having to decode flashing or color-changing LEDs, the new Airfly View adds a built-in screen that displays instructions for each step of the pairing process in one of 24 different languages including Japanese, Arabic, Portuguese, and Polish. The Airfly View is available starting today for $79.99 and includes a carrying case and an adapter for connecting the dongle’s short 3.5mm headphone cable to an airplane’s split headphone jack. That makes it one of Twelve South’s most expensive versions of the Airfly, but the screen is useful for more than just letting you toss the user manual. [Image: The Airfly View’s screen disappears when it’s not in use. The display has a battery level indicator so you can estimate how much of the Airfly View’s estimated 16 hours of battery life remains, and it shows the name of which wireless headphones or earbuds are connected based on how they identify themselves over Bluetooth. That could be useful if you’re juggling a family of flyers who are all traveling with their own headphones. You can stream audio from a single Airfly View dongle to two connected pairs of wireless headphones simultaneously, but Twelve South also says it “supports Auracast broadcast audio, so it is ready for the next generation of Bluetooth headphones.” That will further expand how many devices can receive audio from a single dongle but is dependent on wireless headphones fully supporting that Auracast feature, and not many currently do.

articles.title: Anduril, Qualcomm launch BlueChip, a new kind of US-made laptop | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Anduril founder Palmer Luckey is vowing to bring computer manufacturing back to the U.S. and by that he doesn't just mean assembly, but every individual component, some of which are exclusively made in China today.
articles.body:
Anduril founder Palmer Luckey is vowing to bring computer manufacturing back to the U.S. And by that, he doesn’t just mean assembly, but the production of every individual component, some of which are exclusively made in China today.

Anduril is partnering with Qualcomm to achieve that mission with a new computer called BlueChip, the companies announced Tuesday. BlueChip will be available for preorder in 2027.

While technical details are scant — Anduril hasn’t even finished contracting with all its component suppliers yet, according to Luckey — this first product will be a hardened laptop. It will be designed to withstand the most grueling physical environments and meet the security-conscious needs of the military, government, first responders and law enforcement.

For the first generation, about 90% of its components will be made in the U.S. or in allied countries, Anduril says, most notably its CPU. BlueChip will run on a Snapdragon X Series built at TSCM’s massive new facility in Arizona. The CPU uses the same architecture that powers other laptops, including the Microsoft Surface, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said during the press conference.

“As of right now, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90% U.S. and allied [ally countries], and we have a technical roadmap to get to 100% domestic over time,” Luckey said. “The intent in the long run is to have an option that is made entirely in the United States, 100% domestic. And I mean everything. I mean the displays. I mean the metallics. I mean the the magnetics. All of it.”

Right now, for instance, Luckey says he’s found an American supplier for the glass that covers the display, but the display itself is one of several components he says are only manufactured in China.

While Luckey says consumers are welcome to order a BlueChip — the company may even create a waiting list for interested consumers — this first PC won’t be designed for them. For one thing, as a hardened computer, it will be heavy and have battery-life constraints because of the engineering required to withstand rain, dust, and other rugged conditions.

The bigger point is to offer U.S. government agencies a product that complies with regulations requiring them to buy U.S.-made computers. In this case, the selling point is a transparent supply chain that customers can track and audit.

“These computers are the anti-surveillance computer. You fully control it,” Luckey described in a recent interview. “You know everything that is in it, every single component, and you know every software component that is running on it.”

Anduril is also working to ensure that the Arm-based machine works well with Windows apps, apps built for certain Linux distributions used by the government, and even archaic software that various agencies still run.

While Anduril hasn’t yet announced pricing, Luckey estimates it will cost about 20% more than typical high-end PCs.

“As much as I love BlueChip, if I was just a normal consumer making a rational decision without a kind of patriotic basis, I’d be better off buying a Dell laptop than an Anduril laptop because it’s going to be cheaper. I’m just talking about your average person consumer, right, who doesn’t have any real need for this,” Luckey said.

But Luckey clearly hopes Anduril will eventually make U.S.-made laptops more in line with consumer desires. He said the product is the first in what he envisions as a full line of BlueChip computers, noting that he began his career making devices virtual reality headsets for consumers.

“I’m buying American cars, and then I buy a computer that’s made on the other side of the world, not just China, but you know, Japan, Korea,” he said. “It’s kind of humiliating that as an American and my birthright is computers, in my opinion, because America invented them, that I’m not able to buy an American computer.”

As for the potentially expensive folly of trying to take on China’s electronics components manufacturing industry single-handedly, Luckey joked about his internal reputation for “being a nut” with such big ideas. (He admits that he pushed his board to spend $900 million to build a factory for a jet before the company had even won a contract.)

“This is not one of those things. My investors do not think I’m a crazy person in this particular area,” he said. In fact, rugged computers are already about a $5 billion market .

articles.title: Ford’s sub-$30K electric truck puts the home backup inverter right inside the vehicle
articles.summary: The sub-$30k Ford Fathom features built-in bidirectional charging, offering affordable whole-home backup power and simplified utility grid integration.
articles.body: We’re still a few months away from the official reveal of the Ford Fathom, the automaker’s first next-generation electric vehicle. While we wait, Ford has been whetting our appetite with news about the sub-$30,000 pickup — including today’s announcement about the Fathom’s bidirectional charging capabilities. With an increasing number of EVs coming out with bidirectional vehicle-to-home (V2H) or vehicle-to-load (V2L) charging capabilities, Ford is trying to position the Fathom as a key entrant — and one that simplifies the system by making it an everyday reality rather than a $10,000 luxury perk. Unlike the discontinued F-150 Lightning, which required a massive, expensive external DC-to-AC wall inverter, the Fathom packs the inverter directly into its onboard “E-box” to pump out over 10 kW of AC power natively. The Fathom’s built-in inverter converts its battery power into standard household electricity to run appliances, back up a home during an outage, or feed energy back into the grid. [Image: The Ford Fathom’s E-box supplies up to 10kW of power. Taking advantage of these features will require additional hardware, though Ford aims to make it significantly cheaper than current options. To send power back to the grid, owners will need the Ford Home Power Station. Ford is targeting a 50 percent discount compared to the existing $1,310 Ford Charge Station Pro. For whole-home backup power during a blackout, owners must pair that station with a backup panel. While that combination typically runs around $5,205, Ford is aiming for an estimated $3,123 — a roughly 40 percent reduction — though finalized pricing for both packages is still pending. The Fathom, a $28,000 electric pickup truck, will be the first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, an innovative new system designed to maximize aerodynamic range while also reducing production costs so Ford can make a profitable EV. For over a year, the company has been hyping it as its “Model T moment” that will revolutionize nearly everything at the 123-year-old company. [Image: [Image: [Image: Another barrier to V2H or V2L charging is red tape from public utilities. Ford’s solution was to team up with five of North America’s biggest power companies — Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E); American Electric Power (AEP); BC Hydro; Consumers Energy; and Exelon — which collectively cover millions of customers in the US and Canada. Ford theorized that whatever rules they agree on will likely become the standard everyone else follows. They agreed to cut the paperwork for basic storm backup, use common plugs and software, and make grid programs automatic. Cutting the cost of the Ford Home Power Station and Backup Panel is certainly helpful, but homeowners will still face additional costs related to permitting, electrician labor, and heavy-gauge wiring. These could conspire to keep these bidirectional charging features out of reach for some customers. Still, Ford is intent on keeping the costs low for its new electric truck. With supply chain constraints and trade upheaval, that will remain a central challenge for the automaker as it gets closer to one of the most important vehicle debuts in Ford’s history.
